text:
Collection update! So it’s about to be a year from starting this hobby, I have learned a lot! And I believe we are set for good success!!!

Quite happy with the very few casualties I had, I tought I was not possible to have plants in my room where I have a south facing window on floor 12th with very low humidity ( 20-30% ) an A/C almost 24/7 cuz of the heat, and crazy fluctuations in temperature 18°C–37°C = 64.4°F–98.6°F 🌡️

As a new plant person I would recommend to search on this topics (not in any importance order just random topics that helped my journey) :

- Moss Poles
- Semihydro (Lecca-Moss Method)
- Prop Box
- Hygometer
- Airflow
- Tap water vs Filtered water
- Fertilizer
- PEST PREVENTION
- Humidifier Cleaning
- Anturiums, roomhumidity and leaf expansion
-Tissue Culture
- IKEA Cabinets
-Growth Lights
-Light requirements per specimen
-Light Availability or usage vs Glass
-Corm Sprouting for alocasias
-Silica supplementation for white variegations

text:
My peace lily Bernadette. I've always had a bit of a brown thumb with plants so I've not really had many houseplants. Back in September of 2024 I was gifted a small peace lily and I became determined to keep her alive. I named her Bernadette. I have cats so I took her to work. She did fairly well there. She had a bloom for a while but over time she began to get really yellow leaves and didn't seem to be thriving. I also was not thriving at this job. I had been passed over for a promotion and was feeling pretty down on the whole place. It seemed that Bernadette was mirroring my feelings.

In May I found a new job that I absolutely LOVE and I brought Bernadette along. She is now absolutely thriving! She has four full blooms and a fifth one will soon unfold. I'm so excited about how well she is doing! And that I've managed to keep her alive for two years now. The first pic is November 2025. The second pic is today 17 September 2026.

text:
Baby Costa Rican pitahaya throughout the year. Today is September 20! This is when Spikey (my pitahaya/dragonfruit) first sprouted along with a few other tiny seeds from a pink fleshed dragonfruit (I was struggling with my homework at the time). Spikey grew from a damp paper towel in a plastic bag, except he grew under the sun by the windowsill, not inside a cabinet. Spikey didn't have a cactus yet, he was just this baby thing with two cotyledon leaves, they would open and eventually grow a tiny cactus.

Back in October-November I did remember he was still VERY tiny, but he grew into this blue pot that was way larger than him, when suddenly I dropped him off the shelf to see all the dirt spill everywhere, but lucky for this tiny baby, he survived, and thinking it would be better if he grew in a way smaller pot. And eventually, Spikey grew faster throughout November-January :)

But Spikey got very long, he wasn't the same tiny baby cactus... he grew very tall during the World Cup.

So I never thought it would be a year until Spikey has lived? My cac is so lucky and I wonder how big he will start getting next year, maybe as two times bigger than he is today. Now as a one-year old, Spikey has lived up to his name, now hurting my fingers with those tiny spikes. Happy Birthday, Spikey! 🌵🏜️

(The Flying Dutchman was there for his birthday... my cactus was actually born a day after "Talk Like A Pirate Day" xD)

text:
Tragic Begonia Backstory. All plants are pretty. But these pretty pals also have lore as dark as their edges.

The one with metallic aqua rings is called Red Kiss, the second is a Jurassic Rex who together, apparently, found their way into the world through a story that sounds almost too strange to be true..

There was once a man who admired a woman with a beautiful garden. For years, he watched it grow and began building his own exotic collection of rare plants, hoping to someday catch her attention. He was platonically successful. What she didn't know was that he was collecting them for her.

Eventually, he confessed his feelings. But she didn't feel the same— she was married with children. Devastatingly heartbroken, he later died by suicide.

Afterward, his family discovered the reason behind his collection. Before selling the property, they dug up the rare plants he'd spent years cultivating and gave them to the woman, believing it was what he would have wanted.

She kept some, but couldn't keep them all, so she gave the majority to a friend who shared her love of plants. That friend has cared for them for years, propagating them and passing their offspring along to other plant lovers.

So these plants aren't just surviving.. they're still growing, still being propagated, and still making their way into new homes. And apparently, one of those descendants has now made its way into MY living room.

Naturally, I couldn't say no to a suicide plant. 😂💜

UPDATE: Apparently the seller may have gotten the IDs wrong! A commenter suggested their IDs, which I believe is more accurate. Apparently the plants aren't the rare varieties of Harmony's Fatal Attraction and Dragonsblood that I thought they were, but the backstory is still one hell of a story. 🙈

text:
FINALLY! My first ever successful soil prop. It's a Passiflora Incarnata, the passion fruit plant that's native to the Maryland/Virginia area.

I've tried so many soil props since I started gardening last year and never got one to root when all my water props rooted well and consistently.

Then what happened this year? My water props stopped rooting!

Still have zero idea why. Same water, same method, same time given, same types of plants. TBF it's pretty much only petunias that stopped rooting. Verbena, purple hearts, and Persian shields still worked, but what I wanted were petunias and the kind I bought neither root nor germinate except for two counterexamples out of dozens of attempts. I knew the cultivar may be reproductively challenged but cutting propagation is not something I ever expected multiple petunia plants to give me trouble with.

Needless to say, my confidence has been totally shot after repeated trials and consistent failures across multiple plants. Even ALL of my passion fruit water props are now brown at the bottom, a few of them being former soil props that began failing immediately and had to be"rescued".

This one is the only one that stayed green and it's one of only like three that I kept on the pot perimeter for root watch.

Even if it ultimately fails, I FINALLY GOT A CUTTING TO PROPAGATE IN SOIL. I have now seen with my own eyes that this isn't just something that works for other people, lol.

text:
Wild-Type Phlebodium aureum(Blue Star Fern) really should be more popular. This is my Wild-Type "Blue star fern" that I found as a hitchhiker in an orchid I ordered from Florida. Apparently, the cultivar we see in stores was cultured to favor compact, upright and dense growth, but the wild type doesn't grow like that. You can see I shoved a baby cultivated blue star fern in the pot too but it just hasn't been as vigorous or showy, growing slowly and putting out puny leaves.

My guy has only had about 8 leaves in his life, the first looked like a normal blue star fern leaf, the next got progressively bigger as the rhysome grew. Now I have these monster, dramatic draping leaves.

With how many people love huge leaves plants nowadays and sizing them up, the wild type blue star ferns would be a great addition to ones collection. They just need to be potted in straight sphagnum moss and kept moist, so self watering pots or an orchid pot in a heavy cache pot. They could even be trained to grow up a moss pole too!
